{{Short description|Theorem in algebraic geometry}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], a branch of [[mathematics]], '''Serre duality''' is a [[duality (mathematics)|duality]] for the [[coherent sheaf cohomology]] of algebraic varieties, proved by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]]. The basic version applies to [[vector bundle]]s on a smooth projective variety, but [[Alexander Grothendieck]] found wide generalizations, for example to singular varieties. On an ''n''-dimensional variety, the theorem says that a cohomology group <math>H^i</math> is the [[dual space]] of another one, <math>H^{n-i}</math>. Serre duality is the analog for coherent sheaf cohomology of [[Poincaré duality]] in topology, with the [[canonical line bundle]] replacing the [[orientation sheaf]].

The Serre duality theorem is also true in [[complex geometry]] more generally, for compact [[complex manifolds]] that are not necessarily [[Projective variety|projective]] [[complex algebraic variety|complex algebraic varieties]]. In this setting, the Serre duality theorem is an application of [[Hodge theory]] for [[Dolbeault cohomology]], and may be seen as a result in the theory of [[elliptic operator]]s.

These two different interpretations of Serre duality coincide for non-singular projective complex algebraic varieties, by an application of [[Dolbeault's theorem]] relating sheaf cohomology to Dolbeault cohomology.

==Serre duality for vector bundles==

===Algebraic theorem===
Let ''X'' be a [[smooth variety]] of dimension ''n'' over a field ''k''. Define the '''canonical line bundle''' <math>K_X</math> to be the bundle of [[Coherent sheaf#Examples of vector bundles|''n''-forms]] on ''X'', the top exterior power of the [[cotangent bundle]]:
:<math>K_X=\Omega^n_X={\bigwedge}^n(T^*X).</math>
Suppose in addition that ''X'' is [[proper morphism|proper]] (for example, [[projective variety|projective]]) over ''k''. Then Serre duality says: for an [[algebraic vector bundle]] ''E'' on ''X'' and an integer ''i'', there is a natural isomorphism:
:<math>H^i(X,E)\cong H^{n-i}(X,K_X\otimes E^{\ast})^{\ast}</math>
of finite-dimensional ''k''-vector spaces. Here <math>\otimes</math> denotes the [[tensor product]] of vector bundles. It follows that the dimensions of the two cohomology groups are equal:
:<math>h^i(X,E)=h^{n-i}(X,K_X\otimes E^{\ast}).</math>
As in Poincaré duality, the isomorphism in Serre duality comes from the [[Sheaf cohomology#Cup product|cup product]] in sheaf cohomology. Namely, the composition of the cup product with a natural '''trace map''' on <math>H^n(X,K_X)</math> is a [[perfect pairing]]:
:<math>H^i(X,E)\times H^{n-i}(X,K_X\otimes E^{\ast})\to H^n(X,K_X)\to k.</math>
The trace map is the analog for coherent sheaf cohomology of integration in [[de Rham cohomology]].<ref>Huybrechts (2005), exercise 3.2.3.</ref>

===Differential-geometric theorem===
Serre also proved the same duality statement for ''X'' a compact [[complex manifold]] and ''E'' a [[holomorphic vector bundle]].<ref>Serre (1955); Huybrechts (2005), Proposition 4.1.15.</ref>
Here, the Serre duality theorem is a consequence of [[Hodge theory]]. Namely, on a compact complex manifold <math>X</math> equipped with a [[Riemannian metric]], there is a [[Hodge star operator]]:

:<math>\star: \Omega^p(X) \to \Omega^{2n-p}(X),</math>

where <math>\dim_{\mathbb{C}} X = n</math>. Additionally, since <math>X</math> is complex, there is a splitting of the [[complex differential form]]s into forms of type <math>(p,q)</math>. The Hodge star operator (extended complex-linearly to complex-valued differential forms) interacts with this grading as:

:<math>\star: \Omega^{p,q}(X) \to \Omega^{n-q,n-p}(X).</math>

Notice that the holomorphic and anti-holomorphic indices have switched places. There is a conjugation on complex differential forms which interchanges forms of type <math>(p,q)</math> and <math>(q,p)</math>, and if one defines the '''conjugate-linear Hodge star operator''' by <math>\bar{\star}\omega = \star \bar{\omega}</math> then we have:

:<math>\bar{\star} : \Omega^{p,q}(X) \to \Omega^{n-p,n-q}(X).</math>
Using the conjugate-linear Hodge star, one may define a [[Hermitian]] <math>L^2</math>-inner product on complex differential forms, by:
:<math>\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_{L^2} = \int_X \alpha \wedge \bar{\star}\beta,</math>

where now <math>\alpha \wedge \bar{\star}\beta</math> is an <math>(n,n)</math>-form, and in particular a complex-valued <math>2n</math>-form and can therefore be integrated on <math>X</math> with respect to its canonical [[Orientability|orientation]]. Furthermore, suppose <math>(E,h)</math> is a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle. Then the Hermitian metric <math>h</math> gives a conjugate-linear isomorphism <math>E\cong E^*</math> between <math>E</math> and its [[dual vector bundle]], say <math>\tau: E\to E^*</math>. Defining <math>\bar{\star}_E (\omega \otimes s) = \bar{\star} \omega \otimes \tau(s)</math>, one obtains an isomorphism:

:<math>\bar{\star}_E : \Omega^{p,q}(X,E) \to \Omega^{n-p,n-q}(X,E^*)</math>

where <math>\Omega^{p,q}(X,E)= \Omega^{p,q}(X) \otimes \Gamma(E)</math> consists of smooth <math>E</math>-valued complex differential forms. Using the pairing between <math>E</math> and <math>E^*</math> given by <math>\tau</math> and <math>h</math>, one can therefore define a Hermitian <math>L^2</math>-inner product on such <math>E</math>-valued forms by:
:<math>\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_{L^2} = \int_X \alpha \wedge_h \bar{\star}_E \beta,</math>

where here <math>\wedge_h</math> means wedge product of differential forms and using the pairing between <math>E</math> and <math>E^*</math> given by <math>h</math>.

The '''Hodge theorem for Dolbeault cohomology''' asserts that if we define:

:<math>\Delta_{\bar{\partial}_E} = \bar{\partial}_E^* \bar{\partial}_E + \bar{\partial}_E \bar{\partial}_E^*</math>

where <math>\bar{\partial}_E</math> is the [[Dolbeault operator]] of <math>E</math> and <math>\bar{\partial}_E^*</math> is its formal adjoint with respect to the inner product, then:
:<math>H^{p,q}(X,E) \cong \mathcal{H}^{p,q}_{\Delta_{\bar{\partial}_E}} (X).</math>

On the left is Dolbeault cohomology, and on the right is the vector space of '''harmonic <math>E</math>-valued differential forms''' defined by:

:<math>\mathcal{H}^{p,q}_{\Delta_{\bar{\partial}_E}} (X) = \{\alpha \in \Omega^{p,q}(X,E) \mid \Delta_{\bar{\partial}_E} (\alpha) = 0\}.</math>
Using this description, the Serre duality theorem can be stated as follows: The isomorphism <math>\bar{\star}_E</math> induces a complex linear isomorphism:

:<math>H^{p,q}(X,E) \cong H^{n-p,n-q}(X,E^*)^*.</math>

This can be easily proved using the Hodge theory above. Namely, if <math>[\alpha]</math> is a cohomology class in <math>H^{p,q}(X,E)</math> with unique harmonic representative <math>\alpha \in \mathcal{H}^{p,q}_{\Delta_{\bar{\partial}_E}} (X)</math>, then:

:<math>(\alpha, \bar{\star}_E \alpha) = \langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle_{L^2} \ge 0</math>

with equality if and only if <math>\alpha = 0</math>. In particular, the complex linear pairing:

:<math>(\alpha, \beta) = \int_X \alpha \wedge_h \beta</math>

between <math>\mathcal{H}^{p,q}_{\Delta_{\bar{\partial}_E}} (X)</math> and <math>\mathcal{H}^{n-p,n-q}_{\Delta_{\bar{\partial}_{E^*}}} (X)</math> is [[non-degenerate]], and induces the isomorphism in the Serre duality theorem.

The statement of Serre duality in the algebraic setting may be recovered by taking <math>p=0</math>, and applying [[Dolbeault's theorem]], which states that:

:<math>H^{p,q}(X,E) \cong H^q(X, \boldsymbol{\Omega}^p \otimes E)</math>

where on the left is Dolbeault cohomology and on the right sheaf cohomology, where <math>\boldsymbol{\Omega}^p
</math> denotes the sheaf of holomorphic <math>(p,0)</math>-forms. In particular, we obtain:

:<math>H^q(X,E) \cong H^{0,q}(X,E) \cong H^{n,n-q}(X,E^*)^* \cong H^{n-q}(X, K_X \otimes E^*)^*</math>

where we have used that the sheaf of holomorphic <math>(n,0)</math>-forms is just the [[canonical bundle]] of <math>X</math>.

==Algebraic curves==
A fundamental application of Serre duality is to [[algebraic curve]]s. (Over the [[complex number]]s, it is equivalent to consider [[compact Riemann surface]]s.) For a line bundle ''L'' on a smooth projective curve ''X'' over a field ''k'', the only possibly nonzero cohomology groups are <math>H^0(X,L)</math> and <math>H^1(X,L)</math>. Serre duality describes the <math>H^1</math> group in terms of an <math>H^0</math> group (for a different line bundle).<ref>For a curve, Serre duality is simpler but still nontrivial. One proof is given in Tate (1968).</ref> That is more concrete, since <math>H^0</math> of a line bundle is simply its space of sections.

Serre duality is especially relevant to the [[Riemann–Roch theorem]] for curves. For a line bundle ''L'' of degree ''d'' on a curve ''X'' of [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] ''g'', the Riemann–Roch theorem says that:
:<math>h^0(X,L)-h^1(X,L)=d-g+1.</math>
Using Serre duality, this can be restated in more elementary terms:
:<math>h^0(X,L)-h^0(X,K_X\otimes L^*)=d-g+1.</math>
The latter statement (expressed in terms of [[divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisors]]) is in fact the original version of the theorem from the 19th century. This is the main tool used to analyze how a given curve can be embedded into [[projective space]] and hence to classify algebraic curves.

Example: Every global section of a line bundle of negative degree is zero. Moreover, the degree of the canonical bundle is <math>2g-2</math>. Therefore, Riemann–Roch implies that for a line bundle ''L'' of degree <math>d>2g-2</math>, <math>h^0(X,L)</math> is equal to <math>d-g+1</math>. When the genus ''g'' is at least 2, it follows by Serre duality that <math>h^1(X,TX)=h^0(X,K_X^{\otimes 2})=3g-3</math>. Here <math>H^1(X,TX)</math> is the first-order [[deformation theory|deformation space]] of ''X''. This is the basic calculation needed to show that the [[moduli space of curves]] of genus ''g'' has dimension <math>3g-3</math>.

==Serre duality for coherent sheaves==
Another formulation of Serre duality holds for all [[coherent sheaves]], not just vector bundles. As a first step in generalizing Serre duality, Grothendieck showed that this version works for [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] with mild singularities, [[Cohen–Macaulay ring|Cohen–Macaulay schemes]], not just smooth schemes.

Namely, for a Cohen–Macaulay scheme ''X'' of pure dimension ''n'' over a field ''k'', Grothendieck defined a coherent sheaf <math>\omega_X</math> on ''X'' called the '''[[dualizing sheaf]]'''. (Some authors call this sheaf <math>K_X</math>.) Suppose in addition that ''X'' is proper over ''k''. For a coherent sheaf ''E'' on ''X'' and an integer ''i'', Serre duality says that there is a natural isomorphism:
:<math>\operatorname{Ext}^i_X(E,\omega_X)\cong H^{n-i}(X,E)^*</math>
of finite-dimensional ''k''-vector spaces.<ref>Hartshorne (1977), Theorem III.7.6.</ref> Here the [[Ext functor|Ext group]] is taken in the [[abelian category]] of [[Sheaves of modules|<math>O_X</math>-modules]]. This includes the previous statement, since <math>\operatorname{Ext}^i_X(E,\omega_X)</math> is isomorphic to <math>H^i(X,E^*\otimes \omega_X)</math> when ''E'' is a vector bundle.

In order to use this result, one has to determine the dualizing sheaf explicitly, at least in special cases. When ''X'' is smooth over ''k'', <math>\omega_X</math> is the canonical line bundle <math>K_X</math> defined above. More generally,  if ''X'' is a Cohen–Macaulay subscheme of [[codimension]] ''r'' in a smooth scheme ''Y'' over ''k'', then the dualizing sheaf can be described as an [[Sheaf of modules#Sheaf extension|Ext sheaf]]:<ref>Hartshorne (1977), proof of Proposition III.7.5; {{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0A9X | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A9X}}.</ref>
:<math>\omega_X\cong\mathcal{Ext}^r_{O_Y}(O_X,K_Y).</math>
When ''X'' is a [[local complete intersection]] of codimension ''r'' in a smooth scheme ''Y'', there is a more elementary description: the normal bundle of ''X'' in ''Y'' is a vector bundle of rank ''r'', and the dualizing sheaf of ''X'' is given by:<ref>Hartshorne (1977), Theorem III.7.11; {{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0BQZ | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BQZ}}.</ref>
:<math>\omega_X\cong K_Y|_X\otimes {\bigwedge}^r(N_{X/Y}).</math>
In this case, ''X'' is a Cohen–Macaulay scheme with <math>\omega_X</math> a line bundle, which says that ''X'' is [[Gorenstein scheme|Gorenstein]].

Example: Let ''X'' be a [[complete intersection]] in projective space <math>{\mathbf P}^n</math> over a field ''k'', defined by homogeneous polynomials <math>f_1,\ldots,f_r</math> of degrees <math>d_1,\ldots,d_r</math>. (To say that this is a complete intersection means that ''X'' has dimension <math>n-r</math>.) There are line bundles ''O''(''d'') on <math>{\mathbf P}^n</math> for integers ''d'', with the property that homogeneous polynomials of degree ''d'' can be viewed as sections of ''O''(''d''). Then the dualizing sheaf of ''X'' is the line bundle:
:<math>\omega_X=O(d_1+\cdots+d_r-n-1)|_X,</math>

by the [[adjunction formula]]. For example, the dualizing sheaf of a plane curve ''X'' of degree ''d'' is <math>O(d-3)|_X</math>.

=== Complex moduli of Calabi–Yau threefolds ===
In particular, we can compute the number of complex deformations, equal to <math>\dim(H^1(X,TX))</math> for a [[quintic threefold]] in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>, a Calabi–Yau variety, using Serre duality. Since the Calabi–Yau property ensures <math>K_X \cong \mathcal{O}_X</math> Serre duality shows us that <math>H^1(X,TX) \cong H^2(X, \mathcal{O}_X\otimes \Omega_X) \cong H^2(X, \Omega_X)</math> showing the number of complex moduli is equal to <math>h^{2,1}</math> in the [[Hodge diamond]]. Of course, the last statement depends on the Bogomolev–Tian–Todorov theorem which states every deformation on a Calabi–Yau is unobstructed.

==Grothendieck duality==
{{main|Coherent duality}}
Grothendieck's theory of [[coherent duality]] is a broad generalization of Serre duality, using the language of [[derived categories]]. For any scheme ''X'' of finite type over a field ''k'', there is an object <math>\omega_X^{\bullet}</math> of the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on ''X'', <math>D^b_{\operatorname{coh}}(X)</math>, called the '''dualizing complex''' of ''X'' over ''k''. Formally, <math>\omega_X^{\bullet}</math> is the [[exceptional inverse image functor|exceptional inverse image]] <math>f^!O_Y</math>, where ''f'' is the given morphism <math>X\to Y=\operatorname{Spec}(k)</math>. When ''X'' is Cohen–Macaulay of pure dimension ''n'', <math>\omega_X^{\bullet}</math> is <math>\omega_X[n]</math>; that is, it is the dualizing sheaf discussed above, viewed as a complex in (cohomological) degree −''n''. In particular, when ''X'' is smooth over ''k'', <math>\omega_X^{\bullet}</math> is the canonical line bundle placed in degree −''n''.

Using the dualizing complex, Serre duality generalizes to any proper scheme ''X'' over ''k''. Namely, there is a natural isomorphism of finite-dimensional ''k''-vector spaces:
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,\omega_X^{\bullet})\cong \operatorname{Hom}_X(O_X,E)^*</math>
for any object ''E'' in <math>D^b_{\operatorname{coh}}(X)</math>.<ref>Hartshorne (1966), Corollary VII.3.4(c); {{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0B6I | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B6I}}; {{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0B6S | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B6S}}.</ref>

More generally, for a proper scheme ''X'' over ''k'', an object ''E'' in <math>D^b_{\operatorname{coh}}(X)</math>, and ''F'' a [[perfect complex]] in <math>D_{\operatorname{perf}}(X)</math>, one has the elegant statement: 
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,F\otimes \omega_X^{\bullet})\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(F,E)^*.</math>
Here the tensor product means the [[derived tensor product]], as is natural in derived categories. (To compare with previous formulations, note that <math>\operatorname{Ext}^i_X(E,\omega_X)</math> can be viewed as <math>\operatorname{Hom}_X(E,\omega_X[i])</math>.) When ''X'' is also smooth over ''k'', every object in <math>D^b_{\operatorname{coh}}(X)</math> is a perfect complex, and so this duality applies to all ''E'' and ''F'' in <math>D^b_{\operatorname{coh}}(X)</math>. The statement above is then summarized by saying that <math>F\mapsto F\otimes \omega_X^{\bullet}</math> is a '''Serre functor''' on <math>D^b_{\operatorname{coh}}(X)</math> for ''X'' smooth and proper over ''k''.<ref>Huybrechts (2006), Definition 1.28, Theorem 3.12.</ref>

Serre duality holds more generally for proper [[algebraic space]]s over a field.<ref>{{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 0E58 | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0E58}}.</ref>
